title: Sampled rate curves are read against their uncertainty band, and the fit-quality panel says how well each sample respects it
summary: Each poster shows sampled temperature-dependent rate deviations drawn against 1/T inside a shaded uncertainty band, next to a log-scale objective per sample. The four posters differ in the method that produced the samples; the way to read them is the same: how many curves stay inside the band, what shapes they take, and how the objective behaves.

media.alt: Two panels. Left: deviation of a rate coefficient, in a kappa scale, against 1/T from 0.0004 to 0.0033 inverse kelvin, with a pale blue shaded band between two dashed horizontal limits near plus and minus 1.07; sixteen coloured curves, all horizontal straight lines at different heights inside the band. Right: a red line with markers of a fit-quality objective against sample index 1 to 16 on a log axis between 1e-5 and 1e-2, jumping up and down.

source.caption: Class A sampling: kappa scale, real UQ limits, fit quality per sample
source.note: Group explainer: four posters of the same n-heptane reaction (R1071, as written on the figures) sampled by four classes. Only the generic reading and standard numerical methods are taught; how the project builds its band or objective is not described.
group: 08_muqsac_kappa_classA_poster: Class A sampling (Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse, closed form), 16 samples (representative)
09_muqsac_kappa_classC_poster: Class C sampling (ordinary least squares, closed form), 16 samples
10_muqsac_kappa_classD_poster: Class D sampling (SLSQP, reduced 2-parameter fit), 16 samples
11_muqsac_kappa_classB_poster: Class B sampling (SLSQP, full 3-parameter fit), 10 samples

read_the_figure.question: Do sampled rate curves stay inside the stated uncertainty band over the whole temperature range, and how good is each sample by the objective that selected it?
read_the_figure.axes: Left: x is inverse temperature 1/T in 1/K, from about 0.0004 (T about 2500 K, hot) to 0.0033 (T about 300 K, cold); y is the deviation of the rate coefficient in a 'kappa scale', about plus and minus 1 (the figure does not define the subscript S). The shaded region and dashed lines are labelled as the uncertainty envelope and its limit. Right: x is sample index; y is a squared-distance objective on a log axis, lower being a better match (as the axis label says).
look_at: Count how many coloured curves stay between the dashed lines for the whole x range. In Class A all sixteen are flat lines well inside; in Class C most are inside; in Class D and Class B several curves cross the limits near the ends of the x range.
Look at the shape of the curves: flat lines (a constant offset), smooth monotone curves, or curves with a bend or a hump. The shape follows from how many parameters the fit is free to change.

On the right, how large are the objective values and how spread out are they? Class A values lie roughly between 1e-5 and 4e-3; Class B between about 10 and 50. These are different scales: the two objectives are not necessarily comparable.
Read the title: 'Sample 16/16' (or 10/10 for Class B) means the left panel shows the last frame of the build-up; the sample count differs between classes.
read_the_figure.proves: That for this reaction, each sampling class produces curves of a certain shape and with a certain frequency of staying inside the band. It does not prove which class is better for any downstream purpose.
if_wrong: Curves that leave the band: either the band is not binding for that class, or the sampler does not enforce it.
An objective that is erratic from sample to sample on a log axis: each sample is an independent solve, so no trend is expected, but a big spread shows how much the result depends on the draw.
Panels with different y limits, axes cropped so curves are cut off (as in Class D) hide how far outside the band a curve goes.
must_check: The band and its limit lines are drawn in the same units as the curves.
The same reaction, temperature range and number of samples are used in every panel being compared.
The objective is defined in the axis label and is comparable across the panels being compared.
Axes are not cropped over curves.
Whether the plotted curves are samples or best fits is stated: here they are labelled samples.
as_drawn: Sample counts: 16 (Classes A, C, D), 10 (Class B), as the titles read.
Title objective of the last sample: 5.4e-04 (A), 7.6 (C), 1.0e-03 (D), 28.5 (B). The objective is not comparable across classes unless it is defined identically.
Class B: several curves rise above the upper limit or sink below the lower limit at one end of the temperature range.
Class D: the y axis stops near 1.22 and curves are visibly cut by the frame at the top; some curves reach about minus 1.2, outside the lower limit.

terms.meaning: A reaction's rate coefficient k(T) compared with its nominal value: kappa = k_sample / k_nominal. A kappa of 1 means unchanged. The figures show the deviation from that, in a scale the figure calls kappa scale.
k(T) = A T^n exp(-Ea / R T): a pre-exponential factor, a temperature exponent and an activation energy.
The band within which the rate is considered plausible at each temperature. Here drawn as a shaded region with dashed limit lines.
Choose parameters that minimise the sum of squared residuals. For a model linear in its parameters there is a closed-form solution.
The generalised inverse A^+ of a matrix; A^+ b is the least-squares solution of smallest norm. It always exists and is computed by one matrix decomposition.
Sequential least-squares programming: an iterative optimiser for smooth problems with constraints. It needs many function evaluations and has no closed form.
A closed-form solve is a fixed number of operations. An iterative solve repeats until it converges, and its cost depends on the problem and the starting point.
A squared distance between a sample's curve and a scaled copy of the envelope's shape. Lower is better, as the axis label states.

remember: On an Arrhenius-style axis (1/T) a pure activation-energy change is a straight line; a temperature exponent adds curvature.
A band is only informative if curves are drawn in the same units and clipped nowhere.
A closed-form least-squares solution is one linear solve; an iterative optimiser repeats many evaluations.
Objectives on a log axis can hide large differences: always read the axis labels, not only the shapes.
Different objectives are not comparable across methods unless they are defined the same way.

understand.title: Why 1/T on the x axis
understand.text: Reaction rates depend on temperature mainly through exp(-Ea / R T). Plotting against 1/T turns that factor into a straight line, so differences from nominal are easy to see. The modified Arrhenius form adds a weak curvature from the T^n factor.

understand.title: Why the shapes differ by class
understand.text: A method that may change fewer parameters can only produce simpler curves. Flat horizontal lines mean a constant offset in the plotted quantity. Smooth bent curves come from methods that adjust more than one parameter. A curve with a hump needs the three-parameter form, as in Class B.

understand.title: What the objective on the right means
understand.text: For each sample the objective measures how far the curve is from the envelope's shape after the best possible rescaling. A small value means the curve looks like the envelope. It is a property of the sample, not a ranking of the methods: no trend with sample index is expected.

steps.title: The rate law
steps.note: The modified Arrhenius form with three parameters. R is the gas constant.

steps.title: The ratio to nominal
steps.note: Taking logs of the ratio of two rate laws turns the product into a sum. In terms of x = 1/T it is a constant, a log term and a straight line.

steps.title: Why one parameter gives lines and three give humps
steps.note: If both Delta n and Delta E_a are free, and have opposite signs, the log-ratio has an extremum at T-star, a hump. With only a constant, or only Delta E_a, there is none. This explains why only the full three-parameter class (B) shows pronounced humps. Valid if the plotted deviation behaves like the log ratio; the figure does not define the scale.

steps.title: Closed-form least squares
steps.note: Setting the gradient to zero gives the normal equations. The pseudo-inverse form also covers rank-deficient A, where it returns the solution of smallest norm.

steps.title: Why this is cheap
steps.note: A fixed small number of operations per sample for a few parameters. An iterative optimiser multiplies this by the number of iterations and function evaluations.

steps.title: Fit quality after the best scaling
steps.note: The axis label asks for the squared distance to a scaled copy of the envelope shape f. Minimising over the scale s is a projection: the result is the part of the curve that is not along f. It is zero exactly when the curve has the envelope's shape.

worked.title: Fit quality of a tiny curve
worked.problem: A sample is sampled at two temperatures: delta-kappa = (0.4, 0.6). The envelope shape is f = (1, 1). What is the optimal scale s and the objective?
worked.answer: s is 0.5 and the objective is 0.02. A curve that is flat (0.5, 0.5) would score 0; the objective measures departure from the envelope's shape.

analyze.q: In the Class A poster every curve is a flat line. What does that say about which quantities the method is allowed to change, and what would you check in the Class B poster to see the contrast?
analyze.hint: Count free parameters and look at curve shapes.

analyze.q: The objective axis of Class A runs between 1e-5 and 4e-3 and that of Class B between 10 and 50. Can you conclude that A fits the envelope better than B?
analyze.hint: Is the same distance computed on the same quantity, and are the samples the same size?

analyze.q: Several Class B and Class D curves leave the shaded band. What does that imply about the claim that all samples are constrained to the limit?
analyze.hint: Read the plot first, then the caption.

evaluate.q: Which of the four posters would you trust for a sensitivity study that needs samples inside the band at all temperatures? Justify with what you see.
evaluate.hint: Look at containment in each panel and at how much of the temperature range each covers.

evaluate.q: Critique the figure design: what changes would let a reader compare the four classes fairly?
evaluate.hint: Same y limits, same sample count, an in-band percentage, a shared objective definition.

create: Design a one-number summary per poster, such as the fraction of samples that stay inside the band at all temperatures, and describe how to compute it from the plotted curves.
Propose an animation of the build-up that makes the sampling cost visible alongside the curves.

checks.q: Why is the x axis 1/T and not T?
checks.hint: What does exp(-Ea / R T) become against 1/T?
checks.answer: Because the temperature dependence of a rate is mainly exp(-Ea/(R T)), which is a straight line in 1/T. Differences from nominal then show up as simple lines.

checks.q: A sample has delta-kappa = (0.2, 0.2, 0.2) and the envelope shape is f = (1, 1, 1). What is the objective?
checks.hint: s = <dk, f> / <f, f>, then the residual.
checks.answer: s = 0.6 / 3 = 0.2 and the residual is 0, so the objective is 0 (the curve already has the envelope's shape).

checks.q: Why can a closed-form class generate 100 samples much faster than an iterative class?
checks.answer: A closed-form class does one fixed linear solve per sample. An iterative class repeats function evaluations until convergence, so its cost per sample is many times larger.

checks.q: Two posters have objectives of 1e-3 and 30. Which sampler is better?
checks.hint: Are they the same quantity on the same scale?
checks.answer: You cannot say from the numbers alone. Objectives can differ simply because the class works with different quantities, different numbers of parameters and different sample sizes. Compare them on a common metric first.

checks.q: How would you test whether a sample curve stays inside a band at every temperature?
checks.answer: Evaluate the curve and the limit on a fine temperature grid and check |curve| <= f(T) at every point; report the fraction of samples that pass and the largest exceedance.
